title: Ava and Midge's Watering Plan
markdown:
The sun, a great big golden eye in the sky, had been working extra hard. It beamed and it glowed, warming the earth until even the ladybugs felt a little sleepy. In Farmer Jo’s garden, this meant the flowers were very, very warm. Too warm, in fact. Ava, a bright-eyed girl with a heart as curious as a squirrel’s nose, noticed the pretty petunias and cheerful sunflowers starting to droop. Their once-proud heads hung low, like they were tired of standing up.

“Oh my goodness,” Ava murmured, her voice as soft as the breeze that rustled through the tall grass. “They look so thirsty! They need a good drink of water.” She ran to the garden tap, where cool water flowed. She cupped her small hands, trying to gather as much as she could. But as soon as she lifted her hands from the tap, splish, splash, splosh! The water trickled out between her fingers like tiny escaping secrets. She tried again, and again, but it was no use. Each time, only a few wet drops made it to the edge of the flowerbed before vanishing.

Midge the kitten, a fluffy ball of white and ginger fur, had been watching Ava with wide emerald eyes. Midge loved Ava, and she loved anything that moved, even a dancing sunbeam. She padded over to Ava, her little pink nose twitching. She gave Ava’s hand a gentle nudge, as if to say, I want to help too. Midge tried to carry a drop of water on her tongue, but it just tasted wet. And then that tiny drop was gone. A tiny soft mew, like a sigh made of fluff, escaped Midge. Ava felt a little sad. Seeing her garden friends so droopy, and her own efforts not working well, made her feel like a little wilting daisy herself.

They did not hurry the next look. Ava sat back on her heels. Midge’s tail made a small question mark. A ladybug stayed on a warm leaf and did not bother to fly. The drooping sunflowers kept being tired. Then Ava’s bright eyes found her little red watering can, left leaning against the garden shed. It was shaped like a mini bucket with a long spout. She remembered seeing Farmer Jo use it. She scurried over and dipped it into a shallow puddle that had formed near the water butt. Gurgle, slosh. The water went in, and it stayed in. It was like a tiny portable pond. “It holds the water!” she exclaimed, a little thrill of discovery making her jump.

Then her eyes found Midge, who had spotted a smooth round pebble near the path. Tap, tap, tap. Midge was playfully batting it with her soft paws. The pebble skittered across the dirt, rolling with a gentle rumble. Midge’s tail gave a happy twitch. Ava’s brow furrowed in thought, then smoothed out with a sudden bright idea. A smile bloomed on her face, as sudden and lovely as a poppy. “Midge,” she announced, her voice as cheerful as a robin’s song, “I have a super-duper plan! A helper plan!”

Ava carefully picked up her watering can, making sure to keep it upright. This was the first important part of her plan. She thought, if I fill this watering can with water, then I must carry it very, very gently, so it doesn’t spill. She walked slowly, holding the can steady. She reached the wilting flowers and gently poured the water from the watering can.

Then she looked at Midge, who was still watching the pebble with great interest. Ava gently nudged a flat sturdy leaf she had noticed earlier. “Now, Midge,” Ava whispered, “this leaf is like a little boat for the water! Can you help push it? Remember our game? If you give the leaf a gentle nudge with your paw, then it will roll along the path, right to the flowers!”

Midge’s whiskers twitched with excitement. She understood. Boop! Her paw touched the edge of the leaf. Rumble, rumble. The leaf began to slide along the soft dark earth, heading towards the thirsty flowers. Ava, walking carefully behind, poured a little bit of water from her watering can onto the leaf as it moved. It was like creating a tiny flowing riverbed. Midge, with her playful nudges, guided the leaf-boat, and Ava’s careful pouring kept the water flowing. It was a perfect partnership, as natural as the sun following the moon. Ava’s careful steps and Midge’s gentle pushes made a path of water.

Finally the leaf-boat, steered by Midge’s enthusiastic paws, glided right up to the thirsty flowers. Ava poured the rest of the water from her watering can onto the leaf, and it spread out, soaking into the earth around the flower roots. Slowly, as if waking from a long peaceful sleep, the flowers began to lift their heads. Their petals unfurled, regaining their bright colours. They stood tall and proud once more, their leaves looking refreshed and happy.

Farmer Jo, with his rosy cheeks and a smile as warm as a freshly baked loaf, ambled over. He watched Ava and Midge, his eyes twinkling. “Well done, my clever helpers!” he said kindly.

Ava beamed, her chest filling with a happy warmth, like sunshine on a cool morning. “It’s like a special code, Farmer Jo! We used rules! Like… if I fill the watering can, then I carry it slowly. And if Midge nudges the leaf, then it moves! It’s like… like a garden gate helper, but for water!” She realised that when you have a goal, like watering the flowers, you can break it down into simple steps, like if this happens, then do that.

Midge, beside her, let out a happy purr, rubbing against Ava’s leg. Ava looked at her little friend, then at the now-happy flowers, and finally up at the vast blue sky. Who could have guessed that simple step-by-step thinking, like little instructions, could be so powerful? A whole new world of possibilities opened up in Ava’s mind. And she wondered, with a sparkle in her bright eyes, what other clever rules were hidden all around the garden, and all around the world, just waiting for a curious heart to discover them.
characters: Ava (weather watcher), Midge (white-and-ginger kitten), Jo (rosy-cheeked farmer)
